title: The Genevan psalter
hook: Calvin's churches sang the psalms set to rhyme and tune

segments.voice: Yesterday, only comfort: the Heidelberg Catechism's first question. Your line was my only comfort. When something shook you, what did you reach for? Day one thousand one hundred fifty-nine.

Psalm one hundred, in the King James Bible: "Make a joyful noise unto the LORD, all ye lands. Serve the LORD with gladness: come before his presence with singing." Lovely. Now try getting a whole church to sing that together: farmers, children, people who can't read. Prose has no steady beat. Nobody knows when to breathe or where the tune goes next. In Geneva, John Calvin's church found an answer. They put the psalms into rhyme and regular meter, so anyone could sing them to one strong tune. Today's word: metrical psalm.
screen: `MAKE A JOYFUL NOISE, ALL YE LANDS.`

segments.voice: A metrical psalm is a psalm rewritten in rhymed verse, with a regular count of syllables in each line, so it fits a tune. Calvin wanted the whole congregation singing in worship, not only trained singers. And for songs to sing to God, he argued, you could not do better than the psalms, words he believed God's Spirit had already given. So poets set the psalms into French verse, and musicians fitted them to simple, sturdy tunes. The result was the Genevan Psalter. The idea traveled. English Protestants who had lived in Geneva carried it home, and one of them, William Kethe, set Psalm one hundred like this: "All people that on earth do dwell, / Sing to the Lord with cheerful voice." Count the syllables: eight in each line. That steady count is what lets a crowd move together, breathing in the same places. His words were sung to a tune from the Genevan psalter, and the pairing came to be called the Old Hundredth. Hear what was kept from the psalm: all ye lands becomes all people on earth; gladness becomes a cheerful voice. And hear what changed: now it rhymes, and a child can remember it after a few Sundays. Paul told the Colossians to be "teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord." Churches read that line in more than one way. Some Reformed and Presbyterian churches sing only psalms in worship. Others sing psalms alongside hymns. Either way, the metrical psalm put the Bible's own songbook into ordinary mouths.
screen: `ALL PEOPLE THAT ON EARTH DO DWELL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sing the Old Hundredth, or hum it. If you know the tune, sing the first two lines: all people that on earth do dwell, sing to the Lord with cheerful voice. If you don't know it, say the lines slowly and tap the eight beats of each one on your knee. Then sit in the quiet after the last note. If you pray, let the two lines be your prayer. If you don't, notice what it's like to put your one voice into words that whole rooms of people have sung together. The bell holds the time.
Metrical psalm. A psalm set in rhyme and steady meter, so a whole congregation can sing it to one tune.
Your line: all people that on earth. Today, hum something with a steady beat while you walk or work, and if you know a psalm or a hymn, let it be that. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Reformed and Presbyterian churches sing metrical psalms from psalters, some singing only psalms in worship and others mixing psalms with hymns; "All people that on earth do dwell" to the Old Hundredth tune is sung in churches of several traditions.

notes: Calvin's view ('you could not do better than the psalms', given by God's Spirit) paraphrases his preface to the Genevan Psalter; confirm the paraphrase.
'Poets set the psalms into French verse, and musicians fitted them to tunes' leaves the names out (Clément Marot, Théodore de Bèze; Louis Bourgeois and others). Confirm the summary.

'English Protestants who had lived in Geneva carried it home': the Marian exiles and the Anglo-Genevan psalter. Kethe's authorship of 'All people that on earth do dwell' and its first two lines as quoted are standard; later lines have variants ('fear'/'mirth'), so only lines 1–2 are quoted.
The Old Hundredth tune first appeared in the Genevan Psalter (with another psalm); the script says only 'a tune from the Genevan psalter'. Confirm.
Syllable count (eight per line) is checked against the quoted lines themselves.
'Some Reformed and Presbyterian churches sing only psalms in worship' (exclusive psalmody); confirm fair and unranked.
Original: מִזְמוֹר; Psalm 100:1 Hebrew מִזְמוֹר לְתוֹדָה, KJV heading 'A Psalm of praise'. Confirm vocalization and gloss.

Audit (2026-10-02): 'the churches that followed John Calvin in Geneva solved it' overstated (metrical psalm singing also had roots in Strasbourg); now 'In Geneva, John Calvin's church found an answer.'
